lead: A car must light the road for its driver and show its size and intentions to everyone else. Its lamps fall into four groups: front, rear, interior and special purpose. Each lamp has a colour rule, a switch and a legal limit, and every one sits in the same kind of circuit: battery, fuse, switch or relay, lamp, earth. Only a few universities teach this grouping in depth, but the circuit sums are standard exam questions.
prereq: You need: lamp powers and the 13.2 V rating from lighting technology.

blocks.text: Headlamps give a main (high) beam for empty roads and a dipped (low) beam for traffic. In India the dipped beam's asymmetric cut-off rises on the left, lighting the kerb while keeping light out of oncoming drivers' eyes; the main beam has no cut-off. Aim is set with screws or a levelling motor (see adaptive lighting) and checked against a screen at a test centre.

Position lamps (side lamps) mark the car's width at night. Daytime running lamps (DRLs) are white lamps that come on with the engine and make the car easier to see by day. Front fog lamps are white or selective yellow, mounted low with a wide, flat beam under the fog. Front direction indicators are amber. A headlamp relay carries the lamp current so the stalk switch carries only the relay coil's small current, and many cars fuse the left and right headlamps separately so one blown fuse never leaves the car dark.

Tail lamps are red and come on with the position lamps, typically 5 W each. Stop lamps are a brighter red, typically 21 W each plus a high-mounted centre stop lamp, and are switched by the brake pedal switch. Reversing lamps are white and switched by the gearbox in reverse. Rear direction indicators are amber and flash at 60–120 flashes a minute, about 90 typically. The rear fog lamp is red, about as bright as a stop lamp, and used only in poor visibility. The number-plate lamp is white so the plate can be read.

Interior lamps, the dome, map, vanity, boot and glovebox lamps, are convenience loads. A door switch usually switches the earth side: opening the door earths the lamp and completes the circuit. A body module may fade the lamp out by pulse-width modulation (PWM), switching it on and off so fast that the eye sees only the average. Instrument and switch lamps are dimmed the same way. A failed earth can make lamps on the same earth glow dimly through each other's filaments.

sections.h3: Special-purpose lamps and the lamp circuit

blocks.text: Special-purpose lamps warn or work. Hazard warning lamps flash all the indicators together; the hazard switch has a permanent battery feed so it works with the ignition off. Ambulances, police and breakdown vehicles carry flashing beacons with their own driver. Trucks and tractors carry white work lamps aimed at the job, and some cars have cornering lamps that light the side of the road when the indicator is on at low speed.

The lamp circuit is the same every time: battery → fuse → switch or relay → lamp → earth return (Figure 2.6.1). The fuse protects the wire, not the lamp, so it is sized to the wire and to the load current with a margin. The lamps are in parallel, so one failure leaves the others lit and the currents add. The indicators have their own path: ignition feed → hazard switch → flasher unit → indicator switch → left or right lamps; the flasher sets the rate, and an electronic flasher flashes faster if a lamp fails, warning the driver.

blocks.where: I is the total current in amperes, ΣP the sum of the lamp powers in watts at their rated voltage and V that voltage in volts. A filament lamp at a higher voltage draws more current, but less than in proportion, because its hot filament has a higher resistance.

examples.question: Two 55 W headlamps, two 5 W tail lamps, two 5 W number-plate lamps and 3 W of instrument lamps are on together, all rated at 13.2 V and all on one fuse. Find the current of each group and the total, and choose a standard fuse (5, 7.5, 10, 15, 20 A) with at least 25% margin.
steps: Tail lamps: 2 × 5 = 10 W, I = 10 ÷ 13.2 = 0.76 A. Number-plate lamps: also 10 W, 0.76 A.
With 25% margin: 1.25 × 10.08 = 12.6 A. The next standard fuse above that is 15 A, and the wire must be rated for at least 15 A.
examples.answer: Total 10.08 A (headlamps 8.33 A, tail 0.76 A, plate 0.76 A, instruments 0.23 A); a 15 A fuse.

traps: Treating a 12 V filament lamp as a constant-power load at other voltages. Its current rises with voltage, but less than in proportion; an estimate with the cold-rated resistance at 13.8 V errs on the high side, which is the safe side for a fuse.
Forgetting the stop lamps: two 21 W lamps add 42 W (3.2 A at 13.2 V) only while the brake pedal is pressed.
Swapping main and dipped beam: only the dipped beam has the asymmetric cut-off.
Breaking the colour rules: white or selective yellow at the front, red at the rear, amber only for indicators, white for reversing and number-plate lamps.
Treating the flasher unit as a fuse. It sets the flash rate, about 90 a minute; with an electronic flasher a faster flash means a lamp has failed.

quiz.q: What colour are the rear direction indicators?
Why is a relay used in the headlamp circuit?
quiz.a: The two headlamps take about 8.3 A. The relay contacts carry that current on a short, thick path, while the stalk switch carries only the relay coil current, a fraction of an ampere, so the switch lasts and the voltage drop to the lamps is small.

quiz.q: Two 55 W, 12 V headlamps are run at 13.8 V. Estimate the current using the resistance from the 12 V rating, and say whether the true current is higher or lower.
quiz.a: R per lamp = 12² ÷ 55 = 2.62 Ω; I per lamp = 13.8 ÷ 2.62 = 5.27 A; total 10.5 A. The true current is a little lower, because the filament runs hotter at 13.8 V and its resistance rises.

quiz.q: Why does the hazard switch have a permanent supply, and what would go wrong if it were fed through the ignition switch?
quiz.a: Hazard lamps are needed most when the car has broken down or is parked on the road, often with the ignition off. Fed through the ignition switch they would go dark the moment the key was turned off, so the switch takes a fused feed straight from the battery.

quiz.q: What is the usual flash rate of the direction indicators?
quiz.a: About 90 flashes a minute, within a legal band of about 60 to 120.

quiz.q: Why does an interior door switch usually switch the earth side of the lamp?
quiz.a: The door pillar is part of the body, which is earth, so a single-wire switch in the pillar can earth the lamp when the door opens; the lamp keeps its fused positive feed.

quiz.q: Two 21 W stop lamps and a 5 W high-level stop lamp are rated at 13.2 V. Find the brake-lamp current.

beyond: LED rear lamps light faster than filament lamps, which gives following drivers a few extra metres of warning, and OLED panels make thin, shaped tail lamps. Body control modules now switch lamps with semiconductor switches that also report a failed lamp. Search terms: lamp failure detection, PWM lamp dimming, vehicle lighting installation regulations.
